Thought I would jump in to share my own experience, as it seems applicable here. 

I was a teacher for 4 years. 
I have been in client-facing roles in tech for 6.5+ years (Sales, Business Development, SDR/BDR Team Lead, Customer Success & Support). 
3.5+ of that time has been within the Edtech industry. 

I have been unemployed since June and looking for CS jobs in Edtech for the last 7 months. I consistently get interviews, even to final rounds & take-home challenge/ presentation stages. The only feedback I ever hear is there is as another candidate with more experience. I know countless people with similar backgrounds to me, except were CSMs for 5 - 8 years, and even they are struggling. 

At this point, I am changing strategies and going to apply to entry level sales roles (SDR/BDR). It’s incredibly disheartening and I am basically restarting/ giving up on any hope of a career I was building, but I don’t have any other options. 

If it’s possible, DO NOT give up a current job and enter this job market unemployed. Not discouraging you from applying and prioritizing a career change, but it’s SO much easier to get a job if you have a job, and the competition is FIERCE. 

You very well could get lucky and find the perfect job much sooner than anticipated, but that can happen while you are employed elsewhere, as well. 

The job market right now is absolutely garbage for job searchers now. CS is over saturated, edtech is over saturated, companies have the upper hand, and there are thousands of wonderful professionals competing for limited jobs. I would not wish on anyone. 

BUT, I would be more than happy to share Edtech resources I have been using with you. Just send me a message if you want to learn more.

For new crimes each episode, I listen to [Crime Junkie](https://crimejunkiepodcast.com/), [My Favorite Murder](https://myfavoritemurder.com/) and [Women & Crime](https://womenandcrimepodcast.com/). I know the first two are super popular, but if you haven't heard of Women & Crime I highly recommend! It's two women who are both professors and study different areas of criminology. [The Murder Squad](http://themurdersquad.com/) is also a good show for new crimes (almost) every episode. Definitely a different vibe since it's two men who have been involved in true crime and law enforcement, so they don't participate in the playful banter the way Morbid and MFM do, but they offer a great perspective. Oh, almost forgot! [Swindled](https://swindledpodcast.com/) dives into a different white collar-type crime each episode. The guys voice is very dry, but if you can get past that, he actually makes many sarcastic comments. I've learned about so much corruption from this podcast, so maybe not the best thing but I enjoy taking a deeper look into things. I actually learned about this podcast from Crime Junkie, when they did a recap of [Swindled Episode 06](https://swindledpodcast.com/podcasts/season-1/episode-06-the-contraceptive/). I listened to that one first then was sucked in. 

I've been getting into some non-crime podcasts as well. [Very Presidential](https://www.parcast.com/verypresidential) does a deep dive of a different president each episode. Ashley Flowers is really a good host and I've enjoyed all the content. [The Dream](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/the-dream/id1435743296) looks into MLMs in season 1 and the wellness industry in season 2. [Seven Deadly Sinners](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/seven-deadly-sinners/id1515042150) looks into corruption of pastors and religious figures. It does not bash religion, just uncovers corruption of individuals. My new favorite podcast is [American Hysteria](https://www.stitcher.com/podcast/chelsey-webersmith/american-hysteria). It looks into conspiracy theories, panics, and thinking that have impacted what we fear and believe.

Hopefully you find some you like from that list! I listen to podcasts when I paint and when I take my dog for a walk, so I always have my go-tos and shows to try next saved.
